# English Grammar for the UPSC Vice Principal CRT

## How UPSC tests English in this paper

**The English section is quick marks if you know about twelve rule families; it is not a literature test.**

The syllabus line is only "Hindi and English language skills" (Advt. 51/2026, Appendix-I). The closest previous paper (VP RT, 11 Dec 2022) has not yet been analysed in this folder, so the table below is the standard objective-English pattern used in recruitment tests, not a confirmed breakdown of the UPSC paper:

| Question type | What is really being tested |
|---|---|
| Spot the error (sentence split into 3 parts + "No error") | Agreement, tense, preposition, article |
| Fill in the blank | Preposition, article, tense, conjunction pair |
| Sentence improvement | Idiomatic usage, "No improvement" trap |
| Active/passive, direct/indirect | Fixed transformation rules |
| Synonym, antonym, idiom, one-word substitution | Vocabulary |
| Sentence rearrangement, short passage | Reading logic |

With **one-third negative marking** (each wrong answer loses one-third of that question's marks; a blank costs nothing), attempt only the items where you can name the rule. The rules below are the ones that generate the wrong options.

## Subject–verb agreement

**The verb agrees with the real subject, not with the noun standing nearest to it.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Find the real subject"] --> B["as well as: first subject"]
    A --> C["neither…nor: nearer subject"]
    A --> D["each, every: singular verb"]
    A --> E["a number of: plural"]
    A --> F["the number of: singular"]
    A --> G["Uncountable nouns: singular"]
```

- Words between subject and verb do not change the number: *The **list** of candidates **is** ready.*
- **"as well as", "along with", "together with", "in addition to", "no less than", "and not"**: the verb agrees with the **first** subject. *The Principal, as well as the teachers, **was** present.*
- **"either…or", "neither…nor", "not only…but also"**: the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject. *Neither the Principal nor the teachers **were** informed.*
- **"each", "every", "either", "neither", "anyone", "everyone", "nobody"** take a **singular** verb and a singular pronoun. *Each of the boys **has** done **his** work.*
- **"one of the" + plural noun + singular verb**: *One of the **students** **has** failed.* The clause after "who" agrees with the plural noun: *One of the students **who were** punished has apologised.*
- **"A number of" = plural verb; "The number of" = singular verb.** *A number of teachers **are** absent. The number of absentees **is** large.*
- **Collective nouns** (committee, staff, jury, government) are singular when acting as one unit, plural when members act separately.
- **Uncountable nouns are always singular**: furniture, information, advice, luggage, news, scenery, machinery, poetry, evidence, and hair (meaning all the hair on the head). Never "furnitures" or "an advice"; say "a piece of advice". ("Hairs" is correct only for individual strands: *two grey hairs*.)
- **Plural-only nouns**: scissors, trousers, spectacles, premises, thanks, proceeds, alms. *The premises **were** inspected.*
- **Plural in form, singular in meaning**: news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics (as a subject), measles. *Mathematics **is** my subject.*
- **Distances, sums, periods** as one amount take a singular verb: *Ten thousand rupees **is** a big sum. Five kilometres **is** a long walk.*
- **"Many a" + singular noun + singular verb**: *Many a student **has** tried.*

## Tenses and sequence of tenses

**Time words fix the tense; and a past main clause normally pulls the subordinate clause into the past.**

| Time marker | Tense required |
|---|---|
| yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago | Simple past (*went*) |
| since, for, already, just, yet, so far, recently | Present perfect (*has gone*) |
| by the time X happens, by 2027 | Future perfect (*will have gone*) |
| when X came (another past action already over) | Past perfect (*had gone*) |
| while, at that moment | Continuous (*was going*) |

Key rules:
- **Never use the present perfect with a definite past time word.** *He has joined in 2019* is wrong; *He joined in 2019* or *He has been here since 2019* is right.
- **Present perfect is never used with "ago" or "yesterday".**
- **Sequence of tenses**: a past tense in the main clause takes a past tense in the subordinate clause. *He said that he **was** tired.* Exceptions: **universal truths, habitual facts, and "than" comparisons** keep their own tense. *The teacher said that the earth **revolves** round the sun.*
- **Two past actions**: the earlier one takes **past perfect**. *The train **had left** before we **reached** the station.*
- **"Had better", "would rather", "must", "should"** are followed by the **bare infinitive**: *You had better **leave** now.*
- After **"if", "when", "unless", "till", "as soon as", "before"** in a future sense, use the **simple present**, not "will". *I will call you when he **comes**.*
- **Stative verbs** (know, believe, own, belong, understand, like, seem) are not normally used in continuous forms. *I am knowing him* is wrong.

## Articles and determiners

**"A/an" depends on the first sound, not the first letter; "the" marks a known or unique thing.**

- **"an"** before a vowel **sound**: an **h**our, an **h**onest man, an **M**LA, an **M**.A., an **F**IR, an **X**-ray. **"a"** before a consonant **sound**: a **u**niversity, a **u**nion, a **E**uropean, a **o**ne-rupee coin, a **u**seful book.
- **"The"** is used with: superlatives (**the** best), ordinals (**the** first), unique objects (**the** sun), rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts, plural country names (**the** Netherlands, **the** USA), holy books (**the** Gita), newspapers (**the** Hindu), musical instruments (plays **the** sitar), adjectives used as nouns for a whole class (**the** rich, **the** poor), and nationalities as a group (**the** French).
- **No article** before: names of languages, subjects, meals, diseases, abstract nouns in a general sense, and the words school, college, church, hospital, bed, prison when used for their **purpose** (*go to school*; but *go to the school to meet the Principal*).
- **"Few / little"** = hardly any (negative). **"A few / a little"** = some (positive). **"The few / the little"** = all that there is.
- **"Each"** is used for two or more; **"every"** for three or more. **"Either/neither"** are for **two** only; for more than two use **"any / none"**.
- **"Fewer"** with countable nouns, **"less"** with uncountable: *fewer students, less time*.
- **"Elder / eldest"** only for family members and only attributively (*my elder brother*); **"older / oldest"** for everything, and only "older" takes "than". *He is elder than me* is wrong.

## Prepositions and conjunctions

**Most preposition errors come from a short list of fixed pairs.**

| Correct usage | Common wrong form |
|---|---|
| senior / junior / superior / inferior / prior / preferable **to** | senior **than** |
| different **from**; similar **to** | different **than** |
| responsible **to** a person **for** a thing | responsible **for** a person |
| agree **with** a person, **to** a proposal | agree **to** a person |
| consist **of**; comprise (no "of") | comprise **of** |
| die **of** a disease, **from** a wound, **for** a cause | die **with** |
| married **to**; angry **with** a person, **at** a thing | married **with** |
| discuss, order, attack, resemble, enter, reach + object (no preposition) | discuss **about**, enter **into** a room |
| since + point of time; for + period | since two hours |
| between two; among more than two | between the three |
| in time (before the deadline); on time (exactly) | — |
| beside = next to; besides = in addition to | — |

Correlative conjunctions must be in pairs and placed in parallel positions: **either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and, hardly/scarcely…when, no sooner…than, so…that, such…that, as…as, so…as (negative), lest…should.**

- *No sooner had the bell rung **than** the students left.* Never "no sooner…then".
- *Hardly had he entered **when** the phone rang.* Never "hardly…than".
- **"Unless"** already contains "not": *Unless you work hard, you will fail.* Never "unless you do not".
- **"Lest"** takes **"should"**: *Work hard lest you **should** fail.*
- Do not use **"although…but"** or **"because…so"** together in one sentence.

## Pronouns, adjectives and adverbs

**The case of a pronoun depends on its job in the clause; comparison words follow fixed patterns.**

- After **"than" and "as"**, use the subject form when a verb is understood: *He is taller than **I** (am)*. Exam keys follow this formal rule.
- After **prepositions and transitive verbs**, use the object form: *between you and **me**; let **him** and **me** go.*
- Order of persons: **231 for normal, 123 for admitting a fault.** *You, he and I will go. I, you and he are to blame.*
- **"Who"** is subject, **"whom"** is object: *the teacher **whom** we met; the teacher **who** met us.*
- **"Whose"** can be used for persons and things; **"which"** never for persons.
- **"One…one's"**: *One should do **one's** duty*, not "his duty".
- **"Each other"** for two, **"one another"** for more than two.
- A **relative pronoun** must stand next to its antecedent.
- **Double comparatives/superlatives** are wrong: *more better, most tallest*.
- **"Than"** after comparatives; but **"prefer…to"**: *I prefer tea **to** coffee.*
- Comparing one item with the rest of its group needs **"any other"**: *Delhi is bigger than **any other** city in India.*
- Adjectives that have no degrees: **unique, perfect, complete, round, universal, full, empty**. "More unique" is wrong.
- Verbs of sense (look, smell, taste, feel, sound) take an **adjective**, not an adverb: *The soup tastes **good**.*
- **"Hardly / scarcely"** mean almost not; **"hard"** is the adverb of effort. *He works **hard**; he **hardly** works.*
- **"Very"** modifies adjectives and present participles; **"much"** modifies comparatives and past participles: *very interesting, much surprised, much better.* But past participles that have become ordinary adjectives take "very": *very tired, very pleased*. In modern usage *very interested* is also standard, so do not mark it wrong unless every other option is clearly correct.

## Active and passive voice

**Keep the tense, change the object into the subject, and use the correct form of "be" + past participle.**

| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| writes | is written |
| is writing | is being written |
| wrote | was written |
| was writing | was being written |
| has written | has been written |
| had written | had been written |
| will write | will be written |
| can / must write | can / must be written |

Rules examiners use for wrong options:
- Only **transitive** verbs have a passive. *He sleeps* has no passive.
- **Perfect continuous and future continuous** tenses are not normally changed to passive.
- Imperatives: *Open the door.* → *Let the door **be opened**.* / *You are requested to open the door* (for requests).
- Questions keep the question form: *Who wrote this?* → ***By whom** was this written?*
- Verbs with two objects can take either as the passive subject: *The Principal gave him a prize.* → *He was given a prize* / *A prize was given to him.*
- Some verbs take prepositions other than "by": *known **to**, surprised **at**, pleased **with**, interested **in**, filled **with**.*
- Modal passives: *The form must be filled in* (phrasal verbs keep their particle).

## Direct and indirect speech

**Shift the tense one step back, change the pronouns to the reporter's view, and replace "here-and-now" words.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Direct speech sentence type"] --> B["Statement: said that"]
    A --> C["Yes/no question: asked whether"]
    A --> D["Wh-question: asked + wh-word"]
    A --> E["Command: told to + infinitive"]
    A --> F["Exclamation: exclaimed that"]
    A --> G["Let us: suggested that"]
```

| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| present simple | past simple |
| present continuous | past continuous |
| present perfect | past perfect |
| past simple | past perfect |
| will / shall / can / may | would / should / could / might |
| must | had to (or must for permanent rules) |

Word changes: **now → then; today → that day; yesterday → the previous day / the day before; tomorrow → the next day; ago → before; here → there; this → that; these → those; come → go (only where the sense requires it); last night → the previous night.**

- No tense change if the reporting verb is in the **present or future**, or if the reported speech is a **universal truth**.
- **Questions**: "said to" becomes **asked**; the sentence becomes a statement in word order (no "did", no question mark). Yes/no questions take **"if / whether"**; wh-questions keep the wh-word. *She said to me, "Where do you live?"* → *She asked me where I lived.*
- **Commands and requests**: "said to" becomes **ordered, told, requested, advised**, followed by **"to" + infinitive**; negative commands use **"not to"**. *"Don't talk," the teacher said to the boys* → *The teacher told the boys **not to talk**.*
- **Exclamations**: use *exclaimed with joy/sorrow that*. **Wishes**: *wished that*. **"Let us"** proposals: *suggested / proposed that we should*.

## Conditionals, modals and question tags

**There are three conditional patterns, and the tag always reverses the sign of the main clause.**

| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | simple present | will + verb | real / likely |
| 2 | simple past (were) | would + verb | unreal present |
| 3 | past perfect | would have + past participle | unreal past |

- Formal exams expect **"If I were"** for all persons in Type 2, not "If I was".
- Never put **"will" or "would" in the if-clause**: *If it will rain* is wrong.
- **Inversion** can replace "if": *Had I known, I would have come.*

Modals: **"can"** = ability/permission; **"may"** = possibility/formal permission; **"must"** = obligation; **"should / ought to"** = duty; **"used to"** = past habit now stopped; **"need not"** + bare infinitive = no necessity; **"dare not"** + bare infinitive. The past of "must" in reported speech is **"had to"**.

Question tags:
- Positive statement → **negative tag**; negative statement → **positive tag**. Use the **same auxiliary** and a **pronoun**. *The teachers are here, **aren't they**?*
- **"I am" → "aren't I"**. **"Let us" → "shall we"**. **Imperatives → "will you / won't you"**. **"Let him go" → "will you"**.
- Words like **hardly, seldom, never, nobody, little, few** make the statement negative, so the tag is positive: *He seldom comes late, **does he**?*
- **"Everybody, nobody, someone"** take **"they"** in the tag: *Everyone passed, **didn't they**?*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Look at the statement"] --> B["Positive: negative tag"]
    A --> C["Negative: positive tag"]
    A --> D["hardly, seldom, never: positive tag"]
    A --> E["I am: aren't I"]
    A --> F["Let us: shall we"]
    A --> G["Imperative: will you"]
```

## Vocabulary: idioms, one-word substitutions and spelling

**Learn the high-frequency list; these items are pure recall.**

High-frequency idioms in competitive-exam English:

| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| take with a pinch of salt | accept with doubt |
| a red-letter day | an important, memorable day |
| at the eleventh hour | at the last moment |
| beat about the bush | avoid the main point |
| a white elephant | a costly but useless possession |
| in the same boat | in the same difficulty |
| hit the nail on the head | say exactly the right thing |
| once in a blue moon | very rarely |
| turn a deaf ear | refuse to listen |
| a bolt from the blue | a sudden shock |
| throw cold water on | discourage |
| burn the midnight oil | study late at night |
| call a spade a spade | speak plainly |
| by leaps and bounds | very rapidly |
| a hard nut to crack | a difficult problem or person |

One-word substitutions that suit an education paper: **pedagogue** (a teacher), **pedagogy** (the science of teaching), **curriculum** (course of study), **alumnus / alumni** (former student / students), **philanthropist** (lover of mankind), **misanthrope** (hater of mankind), **omniscient** (all-knowing), **omnipotent** (all-powerful), **ambidextrous** (able to use both hands), **illegible** (cannot be read), **inaudible** (cannot be heard), **truant** (child who stays away from school without leave), **autobiography** (life story written by oneself), **anonymous** (unknown name), **posthumous** (after death), **unanimous** (all agreeing), **veteran** (long experienced), **novice** (beginner), **optimist / pessimist**, **plagiarism** (copying another's work as one's own).

Commonly tested spellings: **accommodate, committee, millennium, occurrence, separate, privilege, liaison, maintenance, harass, embarrass, recommend, questionnaire, supersede, pronunciation, definitely, grammar, bureaucracy, exaggerate, conscientious, guarantee.**

## Sentence rearrangement and comprehension technique

**Find the opener and the link words; most jumbles have one obvious first sentence and one obvious last sentence.**

- The first sentence introduces a noun by its full name; later sentences use **pronouns (it, they, this), articles ("the" scheme) and connectors (however, therefore, also, thus, finally)**.
- Pair sentences that share a noun. Check every option code against two sure links rather than reading all four orders.
- In comprehension, read the questions first, then the passage. Answers must come **only from the passage**, even if your own knowledge differs.
- Vocabulary-in-context questions: substitute each option in the sentence and keep the one that preserves the meaning.

## Common traps

- **Nearest noun agreement**: *The quality of the answers **were** poor* is wrong; the subject is "quality".
- **"The number of" with a plural verb**: wrong. "A number of" is plural; "the number of" is singular.
- **Present perfect + past time word**: *has joined in 2019* is wrong.
- **"Senior than", "different than", "comprise of", "discuss about", "enter into the room"**: all wrong in formal exams.
- **"No sooner…then"** and **"hardly…than"**: wrong pairs. Correct: no sooner…than; hardly…when.
- **"Unless…not"** and **"lest…will"**: wrong. Unless is already negative; lest takes should.
- **"If I was"** and **"if…will"**: formal keys want "if I were" and a present tense after "if".
- **"More better", "most unique"**: double comparison and absolute adjective.
- **"Elder than"**: "elder" never takes "than"; use "older than".
- **Indirect speech with "yesterday" or "did"**: the reported question must lose "did" and change "yesterday" to "the previous day".
- **Imperative narration without "to"**: "told the boys not talk" is wrong; it is "not to talk".
- **"No error" / "No improvement"** is a real option and is sometimes the key. Choose it only if you cannot name a rule that is broken.
- **Tag with "Let us"**: it is "shall we", never "will we" or "don't we".
- **Each other / one another**, **between / among**, **few / a few**, **less / fewer**: the pairs are tested as swaps.
- **Uncountable nouns in the plural**: "furnitures, informations, advices, sceneries, luggages" are always wrong ("hairs" is right only for individual strands).

## Remember for the exam

1. Verb agrees with the real subject; **as well as / along with** take the first subject, **either…or / neither…nor** take the nearer subject.
2. **Each, every, everyone, nobody, many a, one of the** take a **singular** verb.
3. **A number of** = plural; **the number of** = singular.
4. **Furniture, information, advice, news, luggage, hair** are singular; **scissors, trousers, premises** are plural.
5. Present perfect never goes with **yesterday, ago, in 2019**.
6. Two past actions: the earlier takes **past perfect**.
7. After **if / when / unless / as soon as** for the future, use **simple present**.
8. **An** before a vowel sound: an hour, an MLA, an honest man; **a** before a consonant sound: a university, a one-rupee note, a European.
9. **Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, preferable** take **to**; different takes **from**.
10. **No sooner…than; hardly / scarcely…when; lest…should; unless** (never with "not").
11. Type 2 conditional: **If I were…, I would…**; never "will" in the if-clause.
12. Passive = same tense, **be + past participle**; questions become **By whom…?**; imperatives become **Let…be + past participle**.
13. Indirect speech: one tense back; **yesterday → the previous day, tomorrow → the next day, ago → before, now → then**; questions lose "did" and take **if / whether** or the wh-word.
14. Question tags reverse the sign: **I am → aren't I; Let us → shall we; imperatives → will you**; hardly / seldom / never make the tag positive.
15. **Elder / eldest** only for family and never with "than"; **older than** for all.
quick_facts: With 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with' and 'in addition to', the verb agrees with the FIRST subject; with 'either…or' and 'neither…nor' it agrees with the NEARER subject.
'Each', 'every', 'everyone', 'nobody', 'many a' and 'one of the + plural noun' all take a singular verb.
'A number of' takes a plural verb; 'the number of' takes a singular verb.
Furniture, information, advice, news, luggage, scenery, hair (the mass on the head) and evidence are uncountable and singular; scissors, trousers, spectacles and premises are always plural.
Present perfect (has done) is never used with a definite past time word such as yesterday, ago, last year or in 2019.
Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect: 'The train had left before we reached.'
After 'if', 'when', 'unless', 'as soon as' and 'before' in a future sense, use the simple present, never 'will'.
'An' goes before a vowel SOUND (an hour, an MLA, an honest man); 'a' before a consonant sound (a university, a European, a one-rupee coin).
Senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior and preferable take 'to'; 'different' takes 'from'; 'responsible' takes 'to' a person and 'for' a thing.
Fixed pairs: no sooner…than; hardly/scarcely…when; lest…should; 'unless' is already negative so never add 'not'.
Type 2 conditional uses 'If I were…, I would…'; Type 3 uses 'If I had…, I would have…'; 'will' never appears in the if-clause.
Passive keeps the tense and uses be + past participle; a 'Who…?' question becomes 'By whom…?'; an imperative becomes 'Let … be + past participle'.
In indirect speech, tenses go one step back and now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the previous day, tomorrow→the next day, ago→before, here→there.
Question tags reverse the sign of the statement: 'I am' → 'aren't I'; 'Let us' → 'shall we'; imperatives → 'will you'; hardly/seldom/never make the statement negative so the tag is positive.
'Elder/eldest' are used only for family members and never with 'than'; use 'older than'. 'Fewer' goes with countable nouns and 'less' with uncountable nouns.

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:

Neither the Principal nor the teachers ______ present at the inspection.
mcqs.explain_en: With 'neither…nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which is the plural 'teachers', so 'were' is correct. 'Was', 'is' and 'has been' are singular forms that would suit only a singular nearer subject.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin, High School English Grammar: rules of concord (either…or / neither…nor)

mcqs.q_en:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

(A) One of the student / (B) who were punished yesterday / (C) has apologised to the Vice Principal. / (D) No error
options_en: (C) has apologised to the Vice Principal
mcqs.explain_en: 'One of the' must be followed by a plural noun, so it should be 'One of the students'. Part (B) is correct because the relative clause 'who were punished' refers to the plural 'students', and part (C) is correct because the main verb agrees with 'one'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: 'one of the' + plural noun; relative clause agreement

mcqs.q_en:
Fill in the blanks with the correct articles:

He is ______ honest man and ______ university graduate.
mcqs.explain_en: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so it takes 'an'; 'university' begins with the consonant sound /ju:/, so it takes 'a'. Each wrong option chooses the article by the spelling of at least one word instead of its first sound, which is the standard trap.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: use of the indefinite article (sound, not spelling)

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct verb form:

By the time the inspector arrives, the office staff ______ the admission records.
mcqs.explain_en: 'By the time + present tense' points to an action that will be finished before a future moment, which requires the future perfect 'will have completed'. 'Will complete' does not show completion before the arrival, and 'completed' / 'have completed' are not future forms.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: uses of the future perfect tense

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct passive form of the sentence:

The committee has approved the proposal.
options_en: The proposal was approved by the committee.
The proposal had been approved by the committee.
The proposal is approved by the committee.
The proposal has been approved by the committee.
mcqs.explain_en: The active sentence is in the present perfect, so the passive must keep that tense: 'has been approved'. The other options change the tense to simple past, past perfect or simple present, which is the usual wrong-option pattern.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: change of voice, present perfect

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct indirect form:

The teacher said to the boy, "Why did you not do your homework yesterday?"
options_en: The teacher asked the boy why he had not done his homework the previous day.
The teacher asked the boy why did he not do his homework yesterday.
The teacher asked the boy why he did not do his homework the previous day.
The teacher told the boy why he had not done his homework yesterday.
mcqs.explain_en: A reported question needs 'asked', statement word order (no 'did'), simple past shifted to past perfect, and 'yesterday' changed to 'the previous day'. Option 2 keeps question order, option 3 does not shift the tense, and option 4 uses 'told' and keeps 'yesterday'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: indirect speech for interrogative sentences

mcqs.q_en:
Consider the following statements about English usage:

1. 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
2. 'The number of' is followed by a plural verb.
3. 'Scissors' takes a plural verb.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcqs.explain_en: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: furniture is uncountable and singular, scissors is a plural-only noun. Statement 2 is wrong because 'the number of' takes a singular verb; it is 'a number of' that takes a plural verb.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: nouns, number; concord with 'a number of' / 'the number of'

mcqs.q_en:
Fill in the blanks with the correct prepositions:

The Vice Principal is responsible ______ the Principal ______ discipline in the school.
mcqs.explain_en: One is 'responsible to' a person and 'responsible for' a duty or thing, so 'to the Principal for discipline' is correct. The other options swap or repeat the prepositions.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: words followed by particular prepositions

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold:

The staff took the rumour about the transfer **with a pinch of salt**.
mcqs.explain_en: 'To take something with a pinch (or grain) of salt' means to accept it with reservation or doubt. The other options describe either complete belief or complete rejection, neither of which the idiom means.
mcqs.source: Standard idiom lists (Wren & Martin; S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English)

mcqs.q_en:
Match List I (word) with List II (meaning) and select the correct answer using the codes:

List I
A. Pedagogue
B. Philanthropist
C. Misanthrope
D. Ambidextrous

List II
1. One who loves mankind
2. Able to use both hands equally well
3. A teacher
4. One who hates mankind
mcqs.explain_en: Pedagogue means a teacher (3), philanthropist a lover of mankind (1), misanthrope a hater of mankind (4), and ambidextrous one who uses both hands equally well (2). The wrong codes swap pedagogue with philanthropist, or misanthrope with ambidextrous, or both. Remember the roots: 'phil-' means love and 'mis-' means hate.
mcqs.source: Standard one-word substitution lists (S.P. Bakshi, Objective General English)

mcqs.q_en:
Assertion (A): The sentence 'Each of the boys have done their work' is grammatically incorrect.

Reason (R): 'Each' is a distributive pronoun and takes a singular verb and a singular pronoun.

Select the correct answer:
options_en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mcqs.explain_en: The sentence is wrong on both counts and the corrected form is 'Each of the boys has done his work', so A is true. R states exactly the rule that makes it wrong, so R is true and explains A.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: distributive pronouns (each, either, neither)

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the best substitute for the part in bold. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The Principal, as well as the teachers, **were present** at the function.
mcqs.explain_en: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject, 'the Principal', which is singular, so 'was present' is correct. The plural forms 'were', 'have been' and 'are' wrongly agree with 'the teachers'.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: concord with 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with'

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct question tag:

Let us start the staff meeting, ______?
mcqs.explain_en: A proposal beginning with 'Let us' always takes the tag 'shall we'. 'Will you' is the tag for imperatives such as 'Open the door', while 'don't we' and 'won't we' are never used after 'Let us'.

mcqs.q_en:
Choose the correct form for the blank:

If I ______ the Vice Principal, I would revise the examination timetable.
mcqs.explain_en: The main clause 'would revise' marks a Type 2 (unreal present) conditional, which in formal English takes the subjunctive 'were' for all persons. 'Am' belongs to Type 1, 'had been' to Type 3, and 'was' is colloquial and not accepted as the exam key.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: conditional sentences and the subjunctive mood

mcqs.q_en:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

(A) The newly appointed Vice Principal / (B) is senior than / (C) all the other teachers of the school. / (D) No error
options_en: (C) all the other teachers of the school
mcqs.explain_en: Latin-origin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior and preferable take 'to', not 'than', so it should be 'senior to'. Parts (A) and (C) are correct, and 'No error' is the trap for candidates who treat 'senior' like an ordinary comparative.
mcqs.source: Wren & Martin: comparison of adjectives, Latin comparatives followed by 'to'
